events.reason: Facial swelling, shortness of breath and hives after eating at a seafood restaurant

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT RECORD
Date of service: 02/02/2026, arrived 20:10 by EMS. Observation overnight, discharged 02/03/2026 08:30.

CC: facial swelling, SOB, hives

HPI: 26-year-old woman with mild atopic dermatitis and known shellfish anaphylaxis (ED visit August 2025). Tonight at a seafood restaurant with friends she ordered a dish she was told had no shellfish; about 15 minutes after eating, her face swelled, she became short of breath and broke out in an itchy rash all over. Shrimp was later found in the dish. She gave herself her own epinephrine auto-injector at the table and friends called 911. Same picture as August, by her report. Denies stings, new medications or new soaps/lotions.

PMH: atopic dermatitis; shellfish anaphylaxis 2025.
Meds: epinephrine auto-injector prn (one used tonight); triamcinolone 0.1% cream prn; petroleum jelly.
Allergies: shellfish - anaphylaxis; dust mites; pollen.
SH: never smoker, social alcohol. Swim instructor.

Arrival vitals: T 37.0 C, BP 92/60, HR 118, RR 24, SpO2 93% RA.

Exam: Alert, anxious, dyspneic. Periorbital edema. Inspiratory stridor; bilateral wheezing. Urticaria across chest and arms. Heart tachycardic, regular. Abdomen soft.

ED course: IV placed, oxygen by face mask. Epinephrine 0.5 mg IM R thigh (second dose overall). Racemic epinephrine nebulized for stridor, then albuterol nebulizer. NS 2 L. Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV, diphenhydramine 50 mg IV, famotidine 20 mg IV.
Stridor resolved within the hour. 22:15: BP 106/66, HR 100, RR 20, SpO2 97% RA, off oxygen. Wheeze cleared.
Given two doses of epinephrine and airway involvement, kept overnight in ED observation. No recurrence.
08:10: T 36.7, BP 112/70, HR 78, RR 16, SpO2 99% RA. Swelling resolved, skin clear.

Impression: Anaphylaxis due to shellfish (shrimp), recurrent, with upper airway involvement.

Disposition: home. New prescription for epinephrine 0.3 mg auto-injector 2-pack to replace the one used. Follow up with PCP in 2 to 3 days and with allergy/immunology, sooner appointment advised.

documents.title: Allergy and Immunology Consultation
documents.author: allergy and immunology
documents.body:
ALLERGY AND IMMUNOLOGY - NEW PATIENT CONSULTATION
Date of visit: 03/10/2026
Referring: primary care

Thank you for asking us to see Ms. Coolidge, a 26-year-old swim instructor, regarding reactions to shrimp.

History: Two episodes. August 2025: about 30 minutes after shrimp at a friend's home, urticaria, facial swelling, wheeze and hypotension; one dose of IM epinephrine in the ED; tryptase 21.8 ng/mL. February 2026: about 15 minutes after a restaurant dish that turned out to contain shrimp, periorbital swelling, stridor, wheeze and urticaria; self-injected epinephrine at the table and a second dose in the ED, observed overnight. She had previously eaten shrimp without symptoms. No reactions to fish or other foods reported. Mild atopic dermatitis, controlled with intermittent topical triamcinolone. Dust mite and seasonal pollen sensitivity by history. Family: maternal uncle with shellfish allergy; mother asthma, allergic rhinitis; father atopic dermatitis.

Medications: epinephrine 0.3 mg auto-injector; triamcinolone 0.1% cream prn; petroleum jelly.
No antihistamine in the past 7 days.

Exam: Vitals normal. No respiratory distress. Nasal mucosa unremarkable. Lungs clear. Skin: mild xerosis of the hands; no urticaria.

Skin prick testing: shrimp positive, 9 mm wheal. Histamine control 6 mm. Saline control 0 mm.

Assessment: IgE-mediated shrimp allergy with two episodes of anaphylaxis, the second with upper airway involvement.

Recommendations:
1. Strict avoidance of all crustacean shellfish (shrimp, crab, lobster, crawfish).
2. Carry two epinephrine auto-injectors at all times. Written anaphylaxis action plan given and reviewed; copy enclosed.
3. Read labels; communicate the allergy clearly when eating out.
4. Follow up here in one year, sooner if any reaction.

Allergy and Immunology
